title: The Three Baskets
summary: Akbar orders Birbal to fill three baskets with Truth, Illusion, and Falsehood. Birbal returns with three everyday objects that embody profound philosophy.
full_text:
During an evening assembly of philosophers and scholars at Fatehpur Sikri, Emperor Akbar posed a deep metaphysical riddle to his courtiers:

'We speak endlessly of Truth, Illusion, and Falsehood. Can these abstract concepts be captured and held in one's hands? Birbal, I command you: tomorrow morning, bring before my throne three ordinary wicker baskets—one filled with pure Truth, one filled with pure Illusion, and one filled with pure Falsehood!'

The scholars scoffed quietly, convinced that Birbal had finally been trapped by an impossible imperial whim. How could any mortal shovel truth or falsehood into a basket?

The following morning, Birbal walked into the Diwan-i-Khas followed by three palace porters, each carrying a woven wicker basket covered with silk cloth.

Akbar leaned forward with keen curiosity: 'Have you brought what I commanded, Birbal?'

'Yes, Your Majesty,' Birbal answered respectfully.

He removed the cloth from the first basket. It was filled to the brim with coarse white rock salt. 'Sire, this is Truth. Salt is humble, simple, and unadorned. Yet without it, no food on earth has flavor or nourishment. If taken in excess, it bites; if absent, life withers. Truth is raw and unyielding, yet essential for the survival of every soul.'

Next, Birbal uncovered the second basket. Inside rested a polished glass prism and a handful of iridescent peacock feathers that shimmered in colors of emerald, sapphire, and gold depending on the angle of the light. 'Sire, this is Illusion (Maya). From this angle it appears blue, from that angle green, and under shadow it turns dull brown. It dazzles the senses and stirs wonder, yet possesses no permanent reality of its own.'

Finally, Birbal uncovered the third basket. The basket was completely empty, save for a scroll inscribed with courtly panegyrics praising a notoriously cowardly minister as a fearless lion of war.

'And what is this?' Akbar asked.

'Sire, this is Falsehood (Asatya). It promises everything, flatters the vain, and dresses itself in grand words, yet when you reach inside to grasp its substance, you find only empty air and deceit that starves the spirit.'

The assembly broke into spontaneous acclaim. Akbar stood from his throne and embraced Birbal, declaring that wisdom shines brightest when brought down to earth where all can understand.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Three Baskets"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
